titre: ShakeAlert Doesn't Predict the Quake, It Outruns the S Wave
accroche: ShakeAlert doesn't guess anything: it detects a quake already underway and sends an alert faster than the ground itself can shake.
contenu_vulgarise:
An earthquake early warning announces a shake before it arrives. Seen from outside, this looks like prediction. It is not: the earthquake has already begun by the time the alert goes out.

## Two waves, two speeds

When a fault ruptures, energy spreads in two forms. The P wave, a compression wave and the faster of the two, travels at about 3.7 miles (6 km) per second and generally does not produce strong shaking. The S wave and surface waves, slower (about 2.5 miles, or 4 km, per second), arrive next and are generally the most damaging. Today's telecommunications, by contrast, are far faster than seismic waves. ShakeAlert, the USGS system covering the U.S. West Coast, spreads sensors over a wide area where earthquakes are likely, sends their data to a processing center that estimates the location, size, and shaking intensity within seconds, then, if the earthquake meets the USGS alert thresholds, issues a message to technical partners. They produce the alert that prompts people to protect themselves, or trigger an automated action, such as slowing a train or closing valves. The USGS site says it plainly: early warning is not earthquake prediction.

## A real-world test, and its limits

In July 2019, the Ridgecrest sequence, in California, tests a system still under development: a magnitude-6.4 foreshock and a magnitude-7.1 mainshock. ShakeAlert detects and characterizes both earthquakes within 6.9 seconds of their origin, according to the study the USGS later publishes on this sequence, and creates alert messages made available to its pilot users. But public alerting exists at the time only in Los Angeles County, through the ShakeAlertLA app, and no public alert is sent: the shaking predicted for Los Angeles was below the app's threshold (intensity 4.0 on the Mercalli scale). That was accurate for the 6.4 event. For the 7.1 event, public alerts were warranted: both algorithms underestimated the magnitude by 0.8 units, and so the expected shaking.

## What this changes

The system has since expanded: public testing in California starting October 17, 2019, then opening to the whole West Coast on May 4, 2021, for more than 50 million people. But physics imposes a limit: the alert goes out only once the earthquake has started and been detected. The USGS notes that someone farther from the earthquake's origin has more time to receive an alert before shaking arrives. ShakeAlert does not shorten the earthquake, then: it exploits the lead that P waves and telecommunications have over the most damaging waves, all the more the farther one is from the origin.

carte.punch: ShakeAlert doesn't predict anything: it just wins the race against the shaking wave.
carte.idee: An earthquake sends out a fast wave that generally does not produce strong shaking, then slower waves that are generally the most damaging. ShakeAlert detects the first and issues a message before the others arrive. The farther from the origin of the earthquake, the more time one has.

quiz.question: Why can a ShakeAlert warning arrive before an earthquake's strongest shaking?
choix: Because the system forecasts the date and time of the earthquake before it happens
Because the alert travels by telecommunications, far faster than the S wave, after the P wave is detected
Because the sensors measure atmospheric pressure, which changes before every earthquake
Because the USGS deliberately delays the broadcast of real shaking to smooth it out
quiz.explication: The earthquake has already started when the alert goes out: the faster P wave is detected by the sensors, and today's telecommunications are far faster than seismic waves, so the alert can arrive before the most damaging waves. This is not prediction at all, and none of the other mechanisms exist.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happened during the Ridgecrest sequence in July 2019?
choix: ShakeAlert predicted the exact time of the mainshock two days ahead
ShakeAlert detected and characterized both earthquakes within 6.9 seconds
The system was switched off for the entire sequence
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the USGS study on the Ridgecrest sequence, ShakeAlert detected and characterized both earthquakes, magnitude 6.4 then 7.1, within 6.9 seconds of their origin.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why was no public alert sent for the magnitude-7.1 Ridgecrest earthquake?
choix: Because the ShakeAlertLA app did not yet exist in 2019
Because the earthquake occurred outside the area covered by sensors
Because the USGS judged an alert unnecessary for an already-announced quake
Because both algorithms underestimated its magnitude by 0.8 units
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The USGS study shows that both algorithms underestimated the magnitude of the 7.1 earthquake by 0.8 units, and so the expected shaking, which kept back the public alert the situation warranted.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the USGS, who has the most time to receive an alert before shaking arrives?
choix: Someone farther from the earthquake's origin
Someone closer to the earthquake's origin
Someone with the most recent seismic sensor
Someone who downloaded the app first
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The USGS notes that someone farther from the earthquake's origin has more time to receive an alert before shaking arrives: the margin grows with distance, not the reverse.
